hops.title: Find out which of your eyes does the aiming
hops.text: Stretch both arms out, overlap your hands to leave a small triangle between thumbs and index fingers, and frame a distant doorknob with both eyes open. Now close one eye, then the other. Through one eye the doorknob stays in the hole; through the other it jumps out. Sighting dominance is a different thing from the cortical eye preference the lesson measures in single mouse neurons, but it shows the same idea of one eye carrying more weight. In a meta-analysis of 54,087 people from 54 populations, an estimated one in three right-handers was left-eyed in the studies judged free of bias.

sources.citation: Khan FA, Kasturi N, Deb AK. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. 2024;72(8):1181-1185.
Bourassa DC, McManus IC, Bryden MP. Laterality. 1996;1(1):5-34.

hops.title: What knock-in mice revealed about diazepam
hops.text: The knock-in mice in that 2004 experiment came out of a pharmacology question. In 1999, a Zurich group wanted to learn which receptor subtypes carry each of diazepam's effects. Swapping one amino acid in alpha1 erased diazepam's sedative effect in mice while leaving its effect on anxiety-like behavior intact. In a follow-up study, mice with that alpha1 mutation also showed no sedative response to the sleeping pill zolpidem. With the matching change in alpha2, diazepam lost its effect on anxiety-like behavior instead. So the subunit behind the drug's sedation in mice is the same one through which it opened the visual window early. One receptor family, very different jobs.

sources.citation: Crestani F, Martin JR, Möhler H, Rudolph U. British Journal of Pharmacology. 2000;131(7):1251-1254.

image.caption: The receptor subunit behind diazepam's sedation is the one that let it open the mouse visual window early.

hops.afterHeading: Closing the window: brakes, not decay
hops.title: Golgi's nets, dismissed as a staining artifact
hops.text: In 1893 and 1898, Camillo Golgi reported lacy coats wrapping certain neurons in stained sections. His rival Santiago Ramón y Cajal dismissed them as a fixation artifact. A few researchers kept studying the nets into the 1930s; then they got little attention for about fifty years. Modern cytochemistry showed they are real, made of extracellular matrix molecules, although Golgi's theory of the nervous system as one continuous web was still wrong. These are the perineuronal nets. In 2009, digesting them in adult mouse amygdala before fear conditioning kept cue-evoked freezing from returning at follow-up after repeating the cue alone, matching mice conditioned at 16 days old; context fear persisted.
